questions.q: A reciprocal lattice vector $\mathbf G$ is defined by the condition
options: $e^{i\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf R}=1$ for all direct lattice vectors $\mathbf R$
questions.explain: The reciprocal lattice is the set of wave vectors whose plane waves have the periodicity of the Bravais lattice, i.e. $\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf R\in2\pi\mathbb Z$. For a primitive basis $\mathbf a_i$ it is spanned by $\mathbf b_j$ with $\mathbf a_i\cdot\mathbf b_j=2\pi\delta_{ij}$.

questions.q: The Laue condition for elastic scattering is
questions.explain: Constructive interference of waves scattered from all lattice sites requires the momentum transfer $\Delta\mathbf k=\mathbf k'-\mathbf k$ to be a reciprocal lattice vector. With $|\mathbf k'|=|\mathbf k|$ this is equivalent to Bragg's law $2d\sin\theta=n\lambda$.

questions.q: The first Brillouin zone is
options: the Wigner–Seitz cell of the direct lattice
the Wigner–Seitz cell of the reciprocal lattice
the conventional unit cell of the reciprocal lattice
the set of all $\mathbf k$ with $|\mathbf k|<\pi/a$
questions.explain: It consists of all $\mathbf k$ closer to $\mathbf G=0$ than to any other reciprocal lattice point, bounded by Bragg planes. Every Bloch state has a representative in it, since $\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf k+\mathbf G$ are equivalent.

questions.q: In the conventional cubic cell of a BCC lattice, the reflections that vanish are those with
questions.explain: With basis positions $(0,0,0)$ and $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ the structure factor is $S=1+e^{i\pi(h+k+l)}$, which vanishes for odd $h+k+l$. The mixed-parity rule belongs to FCC.

questions.q: For a diatomic chain the optical branch has $\omega\neq0$ at $k=0$ because
options: the two atoms of the basis oscillate against each other, with the centre of mass at rest
questions.explain: At $k=0$ the acoustic mode is a rigid translation (zero restoring force, $\omega=0$), while the optical mode has opposite displacements, so the springs are stretched and $\omega^2=2C(1/m_1+1/m_2)$. At $q=\pi/a$ the branches are separated by a gap because $\omega^2=2C/m_1$ and $2C/m_2$ there.

questions.q: In the Debye model the low-temperature heat capacity follows $C\propto T^3$ because
options: all modes are excited at any $T$
the number of excited modes grows as $T^3$ (a sphere in $\mathbf k$-space) and each carries energy $\sim k_BT$
questions.explain: For $\omega=vk$ and $k_BT\ll k_B\theta_D$ only modes with $k\lesssim k_BT/\hbar v$ are excited; their number scales as $k^3\propto T^3$. The energy per mode is $k_BT$, so $U\propto T^4$ and $C=\mathrm dU/\mathrm dT\propto T^3$.

questions.q: The electronic heat capacity of a metal is linear in $T$ because
options: only electrons within $\sim k_BT$ of $E_F$ can be excited, so their number is $\propto T$
questions.explain: Pauli blocking: states deep in the Fermi sea are filled. The number of excitable electrons is $\sim g(E_F)k_BT$, each gaining $\sim k_BT$, so $U\sim g(E_F)(k_BT)^2$ and $C=\gamma T$ with $\gamma=\tfrac{\pi^2}{3}g(E_F)k_B^2$.

questions.q: For free electrons in 3D, $E_F\propto n^{2/3}$ because
options: $N$ states fill a sphere of radius $k_F$ with $n\propto k_F^3$, and $E=\hbar^2k^2/2m$
the density of states is constant
$E_F$ is set by the lattice constant only
questions.explain: Counting two spin states per $\mathbf k$: $n=k_F^3/3\pi^2$. With $E_F=\hbar^2k_F^2/2m$ this gives $E_F=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}(3\pi^2n)^{2/3}$. The same law applies to metals and white dwarfs.

questions.q: In the Drude model the relaxation time $\tau$ is
options: the time for an electron to cross the sample
the lifetime of the conduction electron
the mean time between collisions of an electron
the period of the lattice vibration
questions.explain: Drude: $m\dot{\mathbf v}=-e\mathbf E-m\mathbf v/\tau$, so $\mathbf v_d=-e\tau\mathbf E/m$ and $\sigma=ne^2\tau/m$. After each collision, the memory of the velocity is lost.

questions.q: The sign of the Hall coefficient $R_H=1/(nq)$ tells you
options: the sign of the dominant charge carriers and their density
questions.explain: In crossed $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ the Lorentz force is balanced by the Hall field $E_y=R_HjB$ with $R_H=1/(nq)$: negative for electrons, positive for holes. $\tau$ drops out in the simple Drude model.

questions.q: In an intrinsic semiconductor $n_i\propto\exp(-E_g/2k_BT)$ with a factor 2 in the exponent because
options: $n=p$ and the mass-action law gives $np\propto e^{-E_g/k_BT}$
the Fermi level is at the conduction band edge
questions.explain: The law of mass action $np=n_i^2\propto e^{-E_g/k_BT}$ with $n=p=n_i$ gives $n_i\propto e^{-E_g/2k_BT}$, since the Fermi level sits at mid-gap. So the thermal activation energy per carrier is $E_g/2$, not $E_g$.

questions.q: The Pauli paramagnetic susceptibility of a metal is nearly independent of $T$ because
options: the magnetic moment of the electron vanishes at low $T$
the exchange interaction aligns all spins
only electrons within $\sim k_BT$ of $E_F$ can flip their spin, giving $\chi\propto g(E_F)\mu_B^2$ (not $1/T$)
questions.explain: Curie's law $\chi=C/T$ holds for independent localised moments. In a degenerate gas, the fraction of excitable spins is $\sim k_BT/E_F$, which cancels the $1/T$ and leaves $\chi_P=\mu_0\mu_B^2g(E_F)$.

questions.q: The van der Waals attraction between two neutral atoms falls off as $r^{-6}$ because
options: the Coulomb interaction between two ions is $\propto r^{-6}$
a fluctuating dipole $p$ creates a field $\propto r^{-3}$, inducing a dipole whose energy scales as $E^2\propto r^{-6}$
questions.explain: The field of a dipole at distance $r$ is $\propto p/r^3$, an induced dipole is $\alpha E$ and the energy is $-\tfrac12\alpha E^2\propto-\alpha p^2/r^6$. The repulsion is modelled by $r^{-12}$ in the Lennard-Jones potential.

questions.q: The lattice constant $a$ of a simple cubic crystal is doubled. The shortest reciprocal lattice vector $2\pi/a$ becomes
questions.explain: $|\mathbf G_{\min}|=2\pi/a$ is inversely proportional to $a$. The Brillouin zone shrinks in the same way, and diffraction peaks move closer together.

questions.q: The X-ray wavelength is doubled for a fixed first-order Bragg reflection (still allowed). $\sin\theta$ becomes
questions.explain: $2d\sin\theta=\lambda$ gives $\sin\theta=\lambda/2d$, which is proportional to $\lambda$. The reflection exists only while $\lambda\le2d$.

questions.q: In a diatomic chain with alternating masses, the masses become equal. What happens at the zone boundary of the original cell?
options: the optical branch gains a lower frequency than the acoustic branch
the gap between acoustic and optical branches closes
questions.explain: At the zone boundary $\omega^2=2C/m_1$ (acoustic) and $2C/m_2$ (optical). If $m_1=m_2$, they coincide and the chain becomes monatomic with half the lattice constant (the zone is unfolded).

questions.q: The atoms of a crystal are replaced by an isotope four times heavier with the same springs. The Debye temperature $\theta_D$
questions.explain: Frequencies scale as $\omega\propto\sqrt{C/M}$ and $k_B\theta_D=\hbar\omega_D$, so $\theta_D\propto M^{-1/2}$, giving a factor $1/2$ for $M\to4M$. Only the inertia changes (the springs are the same), so $v_s$ and $\omega_D$ both scale as $M^{-1/2}$.

questions.q: For $T\ll\theta_D$ the temperature of an insulator is doubled. Its lattice heat capacity changes by a factor
questions.explain: Debye: $C=\tfrac{12\pi^4}{5}Nk_B(T/\theta_D)^3\propto T^3$, so $2^3=8$. Only long-wavelength acoustic phonons ($\hbar\omega\lesssim k_BT$) are excited, which gives the $T^3$ law; the electronic term is separate and linear in $T$.

questions.q: The electron density of a free-electron gas is doubled. $E_F$ changes by a factor
questions.explain: $E_F=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}(3\pi^2n)^{2/3}\propto n^{2/3}$. Doubling $n$ gives $2^{2/3}=1.59$.

questions.q: The effective mass of the electrons doubles at fixed density. $E_F$ and the Sommerfeld coefficient $\gamma$ become
questions.explain: $E_F=\hbar^2k_F^2/2m^*$ with $k_F$ fixed by $n$, so $E_F\propto1/m^*$. The density of states at $E_F$ is $\propto m^*$, hence $\gamma\propto g(E_F)\propto m^*$.

questions.q: A metal is heated from 300 K to 600 K, well above $\theta_D$. Its resistivity roughly
questions.explain: Above $\theta_D$ the phonon number is $\propto T$, so $1/\tau\propto T$ and $\rho=m/ne^2\tau\propto T$ (Bloch–Grüneisen, high-$T$ limit). Therefore $\rho(600\,\mathrm K)/\rho(300\,\mathrm K)\approx2$.

questions.q: The scattering time $\tau$ of a metal doubles at fixed $n$. What happens to $\sigma$ and $R_H$?
questions.explain: $\sigma=ne^2\tau/m\propto\tau$ while $R_H=-1/ne$ contains no $\tau$. So the conductivity probes $\tau$, while the Hall coefficient probes only carrier density and sign.

questions.q: Silicon ($n_i=10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$) is doped with $N_D=10^{16}$ cm$^{-3}$ donors at room temperature. The hole density is about
questions.explain: Full ionisation gives $n\approx N_D$, and the mass-action law $np=n_i^2$ gives $p=n_i^2/N_D=10^{20}/10^{16}=10^4$ cm$^{-3}$. The minority density is thus suppressed by $n_i^2/N_D^2=10^{-12}$ relative to the majority density.

questions.q: An n-type semiconductor is heated until $n_i\gg N_D$. Its carrier densities then become
questions.explain: At high $T$ thermally excited carriers across $E_g$ outnumber the donor electrons, so the Fermi level moves to mid-gap and $n=p=n_i$. This is the reason for the upper temperature limit of devices.

questions.q: The temperature of a Curie paramagnet is doubled. The susceptibility $\chi=C/T$ changes by a factor
questions.explain: Curie's law $\chi=C/T$ with $C\propto n\mu_\mathrm{eff}^2$ gives $\chi\to\chi/2$. Thermal agitation disorders the moments.

questions.q: A ferromagnet is heated above its Curie temperature $T_C$. Then
options: the exchange interaction is switched off
it keeps its magnetisation but loses its domains
questions.explain: Thermal fluctuations overcome the exchange coupling $J$, so the long-range order disappears, but the spins still respond with an enhanced susceptibility $\chi=C/(T-T_C)$. The exchange interaction itself is unchanged.

questions.q: Copper has $n=8.47\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$. Its Fermi energy is about
questions.explain: $E_F=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}(3\pi^2n)^{2/3}=7.0$ eV (with $k_F=1.36\times10^{10}$ m$^{-1}$). Typical metals lie between 2 and 12 eV.

questions.q: With $E_F=7.0$ eV the Fermi temperature $T_F=E_F/k_B$ is about
questions.explain: $T_F=7.0\,\mathrm{eV}/(8.617\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{eV/K})=8.1\times10^4$ K. Room temperature $T/T_F\sim4\times10^{-3}$, so the electron gas is deeply degenerate.

questions.q: Cu K$_\alpha$ X-rays ($\lambda=0.154$ nm) hit planes with $d=0.20$ nm. The first-order Bragg angle $\theta$ is about
questions.explain: $\sin\theta=\lambda/2d=0.154/0.40=0.385$, so $\theta=22.6^\circ$. Remember that the detector angle is $2\theta$.

questions.q: Copper at 300 K has $\rho=1.7\times10^{-8}\,\Omega$ m and $n=8.47\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$. The Drude time $\tau=m/(ne^2\rho)$ is about
questions.explain: $\tau=9.109\times10^{-31}/(8.47\times10^{28}\cdot(1.602\times10^{-19})^2\cdot1.7\times10^{-8})=2.5\times10^{-14}$ s, with mean free path $v_F\tau\approx40$ nm. So the Drude conductivity is frequency independent up to $\omega\sim1/\tau\approx4\times10^{13}$ s$^{-1}$.

questions.q: The magnitude of the Hall coefficient $|R_H|=1/(ne)$ of copper is about
questions.explain: $1/(8.47\times10^{28}\cdot1.602\times10^{-19})=7.4\times10^{-11}$ m$^3$/C. In a semiconductor $n$ is smaller by $10^{6}$ or more, so $R_H$ is far larger.

questions.q: Silicon has $E_g=1.12$ eV. The absorption edge wavelength $\lambda=hc/E_g$ is about
questions.explain: $\lambda=1239.84\,\mathrm{eV\,nm}/1.12\,\mathrm{eV}=1107$ nm, in the near infrared; this is why silicon is opaque to visible light. Photons with $\lambda<1.1$ $\mu$m have energy above the gap, so visible light is absorbed.

questions.q: For Si at 300 K ($k_BT=0.02585$ eV) the Boltzmann factor $\exp(-E_g/2k_BT)$ with $E_g=1.12$ eV is about
questions.explain: $E_g/2k_BT=1.12/0.0517=21.7$ and $e^{-21.7}=3.9\times10^{-10}$. Multiplying by the effective density of states $\sqrt{N_cN_v}\sim3\times10^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$ gives $n_i\sim10^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$.

questions.q: The Dulong–Petit heat capacity $3R$ of a monatomic solid per mole is about
questions.explain: Equipartition gives $k_BT$ per atom per direction (kinetic + potential), so $3k_B$ per atom and $3N_Ak_B=3R=24.9$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$. The value $\tfrac32R=12.5$ would be for a monatomic gas at constant volume.

questions.q: At $T=\theta_D/20$ the Debye heat capacity $C/3Nk_B=\tfrac{4\pi^4}{5}(T/\theta_D)^3$ is about
questions.explain: $\tfrac{4\pi^4}{5}=77.9$ and $(1/20)^3=1.25\times10^{-4}$, so the ratio is $9.7\times10^{-3}\approx10^{-2}$: only about 1 % of the Dulong–Petit value. Only acoustic phonons with $\hbar\omega\lesssim k_BT$ are excited, which gives the $T^3$ law.

questions.q: The Wiedemann–Franz law $\kappa=L\sigma T$ with $L=2.44\times10^{-8}$ W$\Omega$K$^{-2}$ and $\sigma=5.9\times10^{7}$ S m$^{-1}$ (copper) gives at 300 K about
questions.explain: $\kappa=2.44\times10^{-8}\cdot5.9\times10^7\cdot300=432$ W m$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, close to the measured value of 400. $L=\tfrac{\pi^2}{3}(k_B/e)^2$ is universal.

questions.q: Which of the following is a Bravais lattice?
questions.explain: A Bravais lattice looks the same from every lattice point. The honeycomb, diamond and hcp structures need a two-point basis, so they are not Bravais lattices.

questions.q: The number of nearest neighbours in an FCC lattice is
questions.explain: In the FCC lattice each atom touches 4 neighbours in each of the three orthogonal planes, giving $z=12$ (SC: 6, BCC: 8, diamond: 4). The 12 nearest neighbours of the origin sit at $\frac a2(\pm1,\pm1,0)$ and its permutations.

questions.q: The packing fraction of the BCC lattice of touching hard spheres is
questions.explain: Spheres touch along the body diagonal $\sqrt3a=4R$, with 2 spheres per cube: $f=2\cdot\tfrac43\pi R^3/a^3=\pi\sqrt3/8$. The 0.74 is FCC and hcp, and 0.34 is diamond.

questions.q: For the monatomic chain $\omega=2\sqrt{C/m}\,|\sin(ka/2)|$, the group velocity at the zone boundary $k=\pi/a$ is
questions.explain: $v_g=\mathrm d\omega/\mathrm dk=a\sqrt{C/m}\cos(ka/2)$, which vanishes at $k=\pi/a$. The wave is standing (Bragg-reflected).

questions.q: A 3D crystal has 4 atoms per primitive cell. The number of optical phonon branches is
questions.explain: There are $3p=12$ branches in total, 3 of which are acoustic, leaving $3p-3=9$ optical branches. Rule: $3p$ branches, of which 3 are acoustic and $3(p-1)$ optical.

questions.q: The density of states $g(E)$ of the free electron gas in 3D scales as
questions.explain: From $N(E)\propto k^3\propto E^{3/2}$ one gets $g=\mathrm dN/\mathrm dE\propto E^{1/2}$. In 2D it is constant and in 1D $\propto E^{-1/2}$.
questions.source: HS20 MC topic, adapted (not verbatim) (free electrons)

questions.q: A monatomic crystal has $N$ primitive cells. The number of allowed $\mathbf k$ points in the first Brillouin zone is
questions.explain: Periodic boundary conditions allow one $\mathbf k$ per volume $(2\pi)^3/V$, and the zone has volume $(2\pi)^3/V_c$, giving $V/V_c=N$ points. Together with 3 polarisations this gives $3N$ modes.
questions.source: HS20 MC topic, adapted (not verbatim) (counting states)

questions.q: Which of these semiconductors has a direct band gap?
questions.explain: In GaAs the conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum are both at $\Gamma$, so optical transitions conserve $\mathbf k$ (LEDs, lasers). Si, Ge and diamond are indirect.

questions.q: A Hall measurement on a p-doped semiconductor gives a Hall coefficient that is
questions.explain: The Hall field adjusts to balance the Lorentz force on holes, which carry charge $+e$ and have density $p$: $R_H=1/(pe)>0$. For electrons the sign is negative, $R_H=-1/ne$, so the sign of $R_H$ identifies the majority carrier.

questions.q: The mobility is $\mu=e\tau/m^*$. At equal $\tau$ a carrier with a smaller effective mass has
options: a larger density but the same mobility
questions.explain: $\mu\propto1/m^*$: a lighter carrier accelerates more under the same force, as in $v_d=\mu E$ for electrons in GaAs, with $\mu$ much larger than for holes. Hence GaAs electrons ($m^*=0.067m_0$) are much more mobile than holes ($m^*=0.45m_0$) at the same $\tau$.

questions.q: The exchange interaction responsible for ferromagnetism originates from
options: the Coulomb repulsion together with the Pauli principle
questions.explain: Dipole–dipole energies are $\sim10^{-4}$ eV (about 1 K), too small for $T_C\sim10^3$ K. The Coulomb energy depends on the spin through the symmetry of the spatial wave function, so $J\sim$ eV.

questions.q: Van Hove singularities in the phonon density of states occur at frequencies where
questions.explain: The DOS is $g(\omega)\propto\int\mathrm dS/|\nabla_{\mathbf k}\omega|$, which has integrable singularities at critical points (zone boundary, band edges) where $\nabla_{\mathbf k}\omega=0$. Example: in the 1D chain $g(\omega)\propto1/\sqrt{\omega_{\max}^2-\omega^2}$ diverges at the zone-boundary frequency $2\sqrt{C/m}$.

questions.q: In a p-doped semiconductor at $T=0$ the Fermi energy lies
options: between the valence band edge and the acceptor level
questions.explain: At $T=0$ the acceptor level is empty and the valence band full, so $E_F$ lies midway between the valence band edge and the acceptor level; with rising $T$ it moves towards mid-gap.
questions.source: HS20 MC (c), verbatim topic and options, German original translated

questions.q: In the limit $T\to0$ the resistivity of a metal is
options: linear in $T$ because of phonon scattering
independent of $T$ because of phonon scattering
linear in $T$ because of impurity scattering
independent of $T$ because of impurity scattering
questions.explain: Phonons freeze out ($\rho_\mathrm{ph}\propto T^5$ below $\theta_D$), leaving the temperature-independent residual resistivity $\rho_0$ from impurities and defects (Matthiessen's rule).
questions.source: HS20 MC (d), verbatim topic and options, German original translated

questions.q: Einstein model of the specific heat: which statement is FALSE?
options: It gives good values of $c(T)$ at high temperatures.
At high temperatures it agrees with the Dulong-Petit law.
Its density of states is described by a $\delta$ function.
It assumes a linear phonon dispersion, so all modes have the same velocity.
questions.explain: The Einstein model assumes all modes have one frequency $\omega_E$, i.e. a flat dispersion with zero group velocity, which gives the $\delta$-function DOS; a linear dispersion is the Debye assumption. It fails at low $T$ (exponential instead of $T^3$).
questions.source: HS20 MC (l), verbatim topic and options, German original translated

questions.q: A metal has the electron density $5.00\times10^{22}$ cm$^{-3}$. In the free-electron model at $T=0$ the Fermi energy is
questions.explain: $n=5\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$ gives $k_F=(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}=1.14\times10^{10}$ m$^{-1}$ and $E_F=\hbar^2k_F^2/2m=7.9\times10^{-19}$ J $=4.95$ eV, a typical metal value.
questions.source: HS20 MC (m), verbatim topic and options, German original translated

questions.q: Which scattering process does NOT contribute to the finite resistance of a solid?
options: scattering from the ion cores of the exactly periodic lattice
questions.explain: By the Bloch theorem electrons move without scattering in a perfectly periodic potential; only deviations from periodicity (phonons, impurities, defects) cause resistance.
questions.source: HS20 MC (q), verbatim topic and options, German original translated

questions.q: The figure shows the temperature dependence of a carrier density: $\log_{10}n$ (cm$^{-3}$, from $10^{13}$ to $10^{17}$) against $1000/T$ (K$^{-1}$, from 0 to 20). From high $T$ (left) the curve first falls steeply (a dashed line $n_i$ continues this steep fall), then forms a flat plateau at $n\approx10^{15}$ cm$^{-3}$ between about $1000/T=3$ and $8$, and at low $T$ (right) falls again along a straight line of small slope. The figure shows the carrier density of a(n)
questions.explain: A plateau (saturation: all donors ionised, $n\approx N_D$) between a steep intrinsic rise at high $T$ ($n\propto e^{-E_g/2k_BT}$, the dashed $n_i$) and a freeze-out branch at low $T$ ($n\propto e^{-E_d/2k_BT}$, small slope) is the fingerprint of a doped semiconductor. A metal would be flat everywhere; an intrinsic semiconductor would be one straight line in this plot.
questions.source: HS20 MC (a), options verbatim (German original translated); figure described in words

questions.q: The density of states of the electrons of a superconductor with energy gap $\Delta$
options: vanishes for energies in the gap and diverges for energies near the band edge
vanishes for energies outside the gap and is constant for all energies in the gap
diverges in the limit of zero energy and vanishes at the band edge
questions.explain: BCS: $D_s(E)=D_n(0)\,E/\sqrt{E^2-\Delta^2}$ for $|E|>\Delta$ and $0$ for $|E|<\Delta$: no states in the gap and square-root (inverse) singularities at the edges, where the removed states pile up.
questions.source: HS20 MC (b), options verbatim (German original translated); figure described in words

questions.q: A 2D lattice of points is drawn: the points lie on horizontal rows with in-row spacing $p$; neighbouring rows are a distance $p/2$ apart and shifted sideways by $p/2$ (a centred rectangular lattice). Four pairs of vectors are drawn: $a_1=(p,0)$, $a_2=(p/2,p/2)$; $b_1=(p,0)$, $b_2=(0,p)$ (up two rows); $c_1=(2p,0)$, $c_2=(-p/2,p/2)$; $d_1=(3p/2,p/2)$, $d_2=(-3p/2,p/2)$. Which pair is a set of primitive translation vectors?
questions.explain: Primitive vectors span a cell of one lattice point, here area $p\cdot p/2=p^2/2$ (row spacing times in-row spacing). $|a_1\times a_2|=p^2/2$ yes; $b$: $p^2$ (two points), $c$: $p^2$ (two points), $d$: $3p^2/2$ (three points). The cell area is the check: $A_{\rm cell}=|\mathbf a_1\times\mathbf a_2|$ must equal the area per lattice point.
questions.source: HS20 MC (e), options verbatim (German original translated); figure described in words

questions.q: Which of the following shapes can be the unit cell of a crystal lattice? The lattice points sit on the corners of a regular (a) pentagon, (b) hexagon, (c) heptagon, (d) octagon.
questions.explain: Unit cells must tile the plane without gaps. Only rotation axes of order 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 are compatible with translation symmetry (crystallographic restriction), so 5-, 7- and 8-fold polygons cannot tile; the regular hexagon does (the Wigner-Seitz cell of the triangular lattice, also the first BZ of graphene).
questions.source: HS20 MC (f), options verbatim (German original translated); figure described in words

questions.q: Two Laue patterns (spots in a square grid on a screen, spot size proportional to the intensity, black dots mark unobserved reflections) belong to two of sc, fcc, bcc. Pattern (a): along the rows and columns the observed spots form a checkerboard: spots where $h+k$ is even, nothing at the sites with $h+k$ odd. Pattern (b): spots only on every second row and every second column (both indices even); all other grid sites are dark. The correct assignment is
questions.explain: A cubic Laue pattern (plane $l=0$) shows the reciprocal lattice. sc has no extinctions (every site lit). bcc: $S\neq0$ only for $h+k+l$ even, which in the $l=0$ plane is the checkerboard (a). fcc: $h,k,l$ all even or all odd, in the $l=0$ plane both $h,k$ even (b).
questions.source: HS20 MC (g), options verbatim (German original translated); figure described in words

questions.q: In the Debye-Scherrer method a powder sample is illuminated with monochromatic radiation $\lambda_0=2\pi/|\mathbf k_0|$. In terms of the Ewald construction one observes
options: all reflections on a sphere of radius $|\mathbf k_0|$ around the origin of the reciprocal lattice
all reflections on a sphere of radius $|\mathbf k_0|$ around the point $\mathbf k_0$ of the reciprocal lattice
all reflections on a sphere of radius $2|\mathbf k_0|$ around the origin of the reciprocal lattice
all reflections inside a sphere of radius $2|\mathbf k_0|$ around the origin of the reciprocal lattice
questions.explain: The powder contains all crystal orientations, so the Ewald sphere (radius $|\mathbf k_0|$, through the origin) takes every orientation: every $\mathbf G$ with $|\mathbf G|\le2|\mathbf k_0|$ can be reached, each giving a Debye-Scherrer ring $|\mathbf G|=2k_0\sin\theta$. (Single crystal: only the points that lie exactly on the sphere.)
questions.source: HS20 MC (h), options verbatim (German original translated); figure described in words

questions.q: The tight-binding model of a 1D lattice gives the dispersion $E(k)=E_i-A_i-2B_i\cos(ka)$ (with $B_i>0$). The effective mass $m^*$ at the minimum is
questions.explain: $m^*=\hbar^2/(\partial^2E/\partial k^2)$ and $\partial^2E/\partial k^2=2B_ia^2\cos(ka)=2B_ia^2$ at $k=0$ (minimum). A wide band (large $B_i$) means a light electron; $2B_ia^2/\hbar^2$ is the inverse mass, a typical wrong option.
questions.source: HS20 MC (n), options verbatim (German original translated); figure described in words

questions.q: The figure shows a $k$-space isotropic band structure of a 2D semiconductor with parabolic dispersion near the gap: a steep conduction-band parabola with minimum at $E=+\Delta/2$ (large curvature, small mass) and a shallow valence-band parabola with maximum at $E=-\Delta/2$ (small curvature, large mass). Four sketches of the density of states $D(E)$ are offered. (a): step functions with the lower (valence) step small and the upper (conduction) step large; (b): step functions, valence step large and conduction step small; (c): curves falling to zero away from the gap (square-root type); (d): curves rising from zero away from the gap. Which belongs to this band structure?
questions.explain: In 2D the density of states of a parabolic band is a step: $D(E)=m^*/(\pi\hbar^2)$, independent of $E$ (the factor 2 for spin included), starting at the band edge. The flat valence band has the larger mass, so the larger step, and the steep conduction band the smaller step: sketch (b). Square-root shapes (c), (d) would be 3D.
